svg.text: both answer the same question. they differ in what they can tell you at the moment a position opens.
planned as an advisory layer above it

g.text: Why it fired
the trader has to agree before size goes on
Readable on the board: the gate, the
threshold and the value that crossed it.
Recoverable as attribution, not as a
sentence. Weights, not reasons.
Data it needs
minute-level option OI is not vendor-sold
Runs correctly on day one. Each stock is
measured against its own recent behaviour.
Wants hundreds of sessions before its
estimates separate from noise.
Failure mode
how it breaks when the market changes
Visibly. A gate stops passing and the
board goes quiet - which is information.
Quietly. Confidence stays high while the
relationship it learned has already gone.
Changing it
turnaround from idea to validated change
Edit a threshold, replay a recorded day,
read the difference. Minutes.
Retrain, re-validate, re-check for leakage
and drift. Days, done properly.
Cost of being wrong
what a bad call actually costs
Bounded by construction: budgets, small
probes, hard stops, forced close.
Bounded by the same rules - which have to
exist anyway, underneath the model.

svg.text: The hard part of the problem was never the classifier. It was the search.
Finding which few names, out of a universe of thousands of contracts, are being accumulated one-directionally right now is a search over live flow - and the rule
engine performs that search exhaustively, every minute, with a reason attached to every hit. A learned model would be asked to approximate the same ranking, from
far less data, and hand back a number instead of an explanation. So the search runs on rules; learning is queued to re-rank what the search already found.
